title: Substituting for Eubie Blake and Madison Reed's key lesson
summary: Back in Atlantic City, he fills in for the sick Eubie Blake and is scolded by Madison Reed for transposing a song from his own key to E-flat.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Now, okay, how long did you stay in Newark?
About three months.
And then you went back to Atlantic City.
I went back to Atlantic City, yeah.
That's when you went to --
That's when I substituted for Madison Reed for Eubie Blake, when Eubie Blake had me come up there. He was sick in Baltimore.
Uh hunh.
And the reason why I substituted for him, was there wasn't nobody else around there. Because I wasn't raising no hell on the piano, you know.
No?
No. So, what I substituted for him, and I tell you, to give you an episode, an incident of that which taught me another thing about music.

He asked me to play a song for him, 'All That Worries Me is Someone Else Will Be There When I'm Gone'. You see, a song, on account of the war, people sang, they used this song because it was the draft dodgers, you know, and that was the reason why the guy wrote this song. Well, Madison told me, he said, 'I sing that in E-natural.' Well, as I told you, the colored keys were still a nuisance to me. So, E-natural, I had never bothered, I'd rather not play it. Rather play, put in in E-Flat or F, see what I mean? So I put the song in E-Flat, you see?
Uh hunh.
And he went on through the song, he
struggled through the song, but when he'd finished, he comes to the piano and says, "Listen, Sam, when I tell you I want a song in a key, please play it in that key."
Well, I didn't know about absolute pitch. I didn't know that this man would know where he was, you see? Well, I stayed up all night to learn that song in E-natural.
Uh hunh.

But, I never forgot that. Because that was such a slap in the face, that's another one that's like the other -- see, I remembered that, like, I felt about this big. Of course -- because I had had it -- I thought I'd fooled him. Like a lot of other singers, you know what I mean, when you say, "Play that in E-Flat." Well, if you've been used to playing it in F, you want to play it in F. They don't know the difference, it seems a little high. And I say, "Well, maybe your throat's choking you a little bit." Anything, you know. But this man had absolute pitch, as Willy, "the Lion," Smith had absolute pitch.
But, that is not -- that's a gift. You don't have to study for that, or all the studying in the world don't give it to you if you ain't got it. That's a gift, you see what I mean?
Right.

So I went on and I followed this thing through. But after that, I played his songs the way he wanted me to. If I didn't know them, I'd say, "Mr. Reed, give me another day on that song, will you?" Well, if he wanted a special

song and he didn't have to have it that day, I'd work on it all the next day. Unless, there's one time, I was broken down, so tired and worn out, from trying to catch up. But it was building me all the time, you know what I mean? I was scramblin', but it was building me. So that's how those things happened.
